questions.question: A data model constrains what the software can do, and shapes something else as well. What?

options.text: How we think about the problem we are solving
How the storage engine lays out bytes on disk
How many machines the finished system will need
Which query optimizer the database can use

questions.explanation: Data models affect not just how the software is written but how we think about the problem we are solving — which is why the choice of model is a design decision rather than an implementation detail.

questions.question: A data model has two distinct effects on the work of building software. Which two? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: How the software is written
How we think about the problem we are solving
How fast the hardware executes queries
How much disk the data consumes

questions.explanation: A data model shapes both implementation and thought. It determines the structures and operations code naturally expresses, and it also provides the vocabulary in which engineers understand the problem; changing models can therefore change both code and reasoning.

optionExplanations.a: A data model determines the structures, relationships, and operations that application code can express naturally. Changing the model therefore changes interfaces and implementation even when the underlying facts stay the same.
optionExplanations.b: A model supplies the concepts and vocabulary used to frame the domain, so it shapes reasoning before code is written. A graph, document, and relational view can make different aspects of the same problem salient.
optionExplanations.c: Hardware and query-engine implementation largely determine execution speed; choosing a model does not mechanically set the CPU's performance. A poor model fit may cause inefficient queries, but that is an indirect workload interaction.
optionExplanations.d: Encoding and storage layout affect bytes consumed, while the abstract data model alone does not fix physical size. The same relational or document data can be encoded with very different overheads.

questions.question: Most applications are built by layering one data model on another. What is the single key question you ask at each layer?

options.text: How fast can this particular layer be made to run?
How is it represented in terms of the next-lower layer?
Which team owns and operates this particular layer?
Can this layer be replaced independently of the others?

questions.explanation: At every layer, ask how its concepts are represented using the layer below—for example, application objects as JSON, JSON as bytes, and bytes as electrical or magnetic state. A good abstraction hides lower-level complexity while preserving the operations the upper layer needs.

questions.question: Order the four layers of data representation from highest to lowest.

options.text: Application objects; a general-purpose model (JSON, tables, graph); bytes; electrical currents
A general-purpose model; application objects; bytes; electrical currents and light
Bytes on disk; application objects; a general-purpose model; electrical currents
Electrical currents; bytes on disk; a general-purpose model; application objects

questions.explanation: The lowest layer is electrical currents, pulses of light, magnetic fields. The application layer is often specific to your application; the general-purpose data model may allow the data to be queried, searched, manipulated, and processed.

questions.question: What organizational benefit comes from layering data models?

options.text: It reduces the number of engineers a project needs to employ overall
It lets database vendor engineers and application developers work together effectively
It makes the resulting system measurably faster at runtime in production
It removes the need to document the interfaces between the teams

questions.explanation: The clean data model between layers is what makes the division of labour possible.

questions.question: Every data model embodies assumptions about how it will be used. Which consequences follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some kinds of usage are easy, others are not supported
Some operations are fast, others perform badly
Some data transformations feel natural, others are awkward
Some models are free, others require commercial licensing

questions.explanation: A model makes some relationships and operations natural while making others awkward or slow. Choosing a model is therefore a workload decision: it should fit the application's common access patterns and expected evolution, not merely store the current data shape.

optionExplanations.a: Every model privileges particular relationships and access patterns, so some queries map directly to its primitives while others may not be supported. This is why model selection must follow the intended workload.
optionExplanations.b: Operations aligned with a model's indexes and structure can be efficient, while mismatched access patterns require scans, joins, or application work. A model is therefore also a performance choice.
optionExplanations.c: Tree-shaped documents make nested one-to-many data natural, while dense cross-links are often more natural in graphs or relations. The awkwardness reflects the model's assumptions rather than an inability to store the bytes.
optionExplanations.d: Licensing is a property of a product and vendor, not of the relational, document, or graph model itself. Open-source and commercial implementations exist for several models.

questions.question: What is the difference between choosing a data model and choosing a storage engine?

options.text: The model is a vendor product choice; the engine is a query language choice
The model is how you express and query data; the engine is how bytes are laid out
The model fixes the on-disk layout; the engine decides which joins are allowed
They are two names for one decision, taken at two different points in time

questions.explanation: A data model — relational, document, graph — is the layer you write the application against. Storage and retrieval is one layer down: how that model is represented in bytes. The same model can sit on very different engines, which is exactly why the two decisions separate.

questions.question: Give the relational model's own terms, their SQL equivalents, and one important property of a relation.

options.text: Relations become tables, tuples become rows; a relation is an unordered collection
Relations become rows, tuples become tables; a relation is an ordered collection
Relations become schemas, tuples become columns; ordering is significant
Relations become indexes, tuples become keys; the collection is sorted by key

questions.explanation: Codd proposed the model in 1970. Unorderedness is load-bearing: it is exactly what lets the query optimizer reorder work, as the declarative-query section later argues.

questions.question: Which workloads were relational databases originally built to serve?

options.text: Scientific simulation on supercomputers
Military logistics requiring a special consistency model
Mainframe business transactions and batch processing
Early web applications and search engines

questions.explanation: Relational databases grew from business transaction and batch-processing workloads on mainframes. Those origins now look ordinary precisely because tables and declarative queries generalized successfully to many later domains.

questions.question: What did other databases of the relational era force developers to do, and how does that frame the relational model's goal?

options.text: They forced thinking about the internal representation; relational hid it behind an interface
They forced developers to write out every single query by hand in SQL
They forced developers to begin and end every transaction manually in code
They forced developers to shard their data across several machines by hand

questions.explanation: The relational model was an abstraction play from the start: hiding the implementation detail behind a cleaner interface.

questions.question: Match each challenger to its era: the network and hierarchical models, object databases, XML databases.

options.text: Network/hierarchical 1970s-early 80s; object databases late 80s-early 90s; XML early 2000s
Object databases in the 1970s; network/hierarchical in the 1990s; XML in the 2010s
XML in the 1980s; object databases in the 1990s; network/hierarchical in the 2000s
All three of them emerged together during the 1990s and competed directly

questions.explanation: Object databases came and went again; XML databases have only seen niche adoption. Each competitor generated a lot of hype in its time, but it never lasted.

questions.question: What happened to computing that could have killed relational databases, and what happened instead?

options.text: Disks became cheap, so normalization stopped being worth its complexity
Computing diversified enormously, yet the relational model generalized to fit it
SQL was standardized, which locked in the incumbent vendors
Mainframes gave way to minicomputers that ran only relational software

questions.explanation: Computers became vastly more powerful, networked, and diverse, yet relational tables and declarative queries adapted to many new domains. That broad generality, rather than merely incumbent lock-in, explains much of the model's longevity.

questions.question: Where did the name 'NoSQL' actually come from?

options.text: A 1998 research paper proposing non-relational storage for the web
A 2009 Twitter hashtag for a meetup, later reread as 'Not Only SQL'
A marketing campaign run by the makers of MongoDB
An internal Google codename that leaked into public use

questions.explanation: The name began as a 2009 Twitter hashtag for a meetup about open-source, distributed, nonrelational databases. It was later reinterpreted as “Not Only SQL,” a more useful label because these systems are defined by varied goals rather than a single rejection of SQL.

questions.question: Which forces drove NoSQL adoption? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A need for greater scalability — very large datasets or very high write throughput
A widespread preference for free and open source over commercial products
Specialized query operations the relational model supports poorly, and schema frustration
A shortage of engineers who knew SQL well enough to use relational databases

questions.explanation: Four forces in total: scalability, open source preference, specialized queries, and frustration with the restrictiveness of relational schemas.

optionExplanations.a: Some NoSQL systems targeted datasets and write rates that were difficult or expensive to handle with the relational products then in use. Horizontal scale and high throughput were explicit adoption drivers.
optionExplanations.b: Many teams preferred freely available open-source systems over expensive commercial database products. That organizational and economic preference contributed to adoption independently of data modeling.
optionExplanations.c: Specialized access patterns and frustration with rigid relational schemas encouraged systems with different query models and schema flexibility. The force was not that relations were useless, but that some workloads fit poorly.
optionExplanations.d: A shortage of SQL knowledge is not identified as a driver; SQL was already widespread and well understood. NoSQL systems often introduced unfamiliar APIs, so they did not simply solve a training shortage.

questions.question: Define polyglot persistence, and give the reasoning behind it.

options.text: Relational will coexist with nonrelational stores, because requirements differ per application
Every application should settle on exactly one database chosen carefully up front
All data should eventually migrate to a single polyglot database engine
Applications should speak several query languages against one shared store

questions.explanation: Different workloads benefit from different data models and operational trade-offs. Polyglot persistence therefore predicts coexistence: an organization may use relational and nonrelational stores where each is the better fit, rather than expecting either family to replace the other.

questions.question: Explain the electronics metaphor behind 'impedance mismatch'.

options.text: Impedance is resistance, so the metaphor is about queries running slowly
Power transfer is maximized when impedances match; a mismatch causes reflections
It refers to voltage differences between two connected components
It comes from mechanical engineering, describing friction between moving parts

questions.explanation: The analogue is the awkward translation layer required between the objects in application code and the database model of tables, rows and columns.

questions.question: Which ORM frameworks are the standard examples, and what do they achieve and fail to achieve?

options.text: ActiveRecord and Hibernate; they cut boilerplate but can't hide the model differences
Entity Framework and SQLAlchemy; they fully eliminate the impedance mismatch
ActiveRecord and Hibernate; they make relational databases largely obsolete
Django ORM and Sequelize; they help with reads but not with writes

questions.explanation: Reduced boilerplate, not removed mismatch — a precise and limited claim.

questions.question: In the LinkedIn résumé example, first_name and last_name are columns on the users table, but positions, education and contact_info are not. What rule decides this?

options.text: Cardinality: exactly-once fields become columns, varying-number become one-to-many
Data type: strings become columns, everything else moves to separate tables
Query frequency: the most frequently read fields are promoted to columns
Mutability: fields that never change become columns on the main table

questions.explanation: Cardinality drives the schema: first_name and last_name appear exactly once per user, the others occur in varying numbers.

questions.question: Which three options exist for representing the résumé's one-to-many relationships in a relational schema? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Normalized separate tables with a foreign key — traditional prior to SQL:1999
Structured XML or JSON columns, queryable and indexable inside the document
An opaque text column, leaving the application to interpret its contents
A graph edge table linking each résumé section to its parent profile

questions.explanation: Three escalating levels of database involvement — from fully normalized to fully opaque. XML support is named in Oracle, IBM DB2, MS SQL Server and PostgreSQL; JSON in DB2, MySQL and PostgreSQL.

optionExplanations.a: Separate child tables with foreign keys represent one-to-many relationships explicitly and let the database enforce and query them. This was the conventional relational design before structured document-valued columns became common.
optionExplanations.b: XML or JSON columns can keep the nested items together while still allowing supported databases to inspect and index their contents. This trades normalized rows for document locality inside a relational system.
optionExplanations.c: An opaque text field can hold the entire nested representation, but the application must parse, validate, and query it itself. It is a valid representation with the least database involvement.
optionExplanations.d: A graph-style edge table is not a distinct fourth representation in the enumerated relational choices; for this parent-child relationship it reduces to another normalized link table. Introducing graph terminology does not create a separate storage category.

questions.question: What specifically do you lose by storing the document in a plain text column rather than a structured or JSON column?

options.text: You typically cannot use the database to query for values inside that column
You lose transactional guarantees on writes to that column
You lose the ability to replicate that column to followers
You lose the ability to update the column after it is written

questions.explanation: The database can store it but not see into it, so all filtering and indexing on its contents must move to the application.

questions.question: Why is a JSON representation 'quite appropriate' for a résumé, and what does JSON have over XML?

options.text: Because JSON enforces a schema where XML leaves structure unchecked
Because JSON supports joins natively and XML does not
A résumé is mostly self-contained; and JSON is much simpler than XML
Because JSON compresses considerably better than equivalent XML

questions.explanation: Self-containedness is the structural argument; simplicity is the ergonomic one. Document-oriented databases named include MongoDB, RethinkDB, CouchDB and Espresso.

questions.question: Two caveats qualify the claim that a JSON document model reduces the impedance mismatch. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: JSON has problems as an encoding format, apart from its merits as a model
Its lack of a schema is often cited as an advantage, which is debatable
JSON cannot represent nested structures beyond two levels deep
JSON is not supported by any of the major relational databases

questions.explanation: JSON's nested model may reduce the object-relational impedance mismatch, but that is separate from JSON's weaknesses as a wire encoding. Also, schema flexibility is a trade-off rather than an unconditional advantage: less enforcement can simplify evolution while moving validation responsibility into application code.

optionExplanations.a: JSON's usefulness as a nested data model is separate from its wire-format limitations, such as ambiguity around numbers and binary data. Reduced impedance mismatch therefore does not imply a perfect encoding.
optionExplanations.b: Schema flexibility moves enforcement from the database toward readers and application code. That can ease heterogeneous evolution, but it can also permit inconsistent records, so calling it an unconditional advantage is debatable.
optionExplanations.c: JSON arrays and objects can be nested to arbitrary practical depths; it has no two-level structural limit. Deep nesting may be inconvenient, but it is not a format prohibition.
optionExplanations.d: Major relational databases support JSON or XML columns and functions, with varying indexing and validation capabilities. Lack of relational support is therefore not a valid caveat.

questions.question: Compare fetching a whole profile in the relational schema versus the JSON representation.

options.text: Relational needs multiple queries or a messy multiway join; JSON needs one
Each needs exactly one query; only the shape of the result differs
JSON needs more queries, since nested items resolve separately
Relational is always faster, because its indexes are better optimized

questions.explanation: A JSON document can place an entire profile in one record, avoiding several relational queries or a large join. That locality helps only when reads need much of the document; loading or rewriting a large document for one small field can erase the advantage.

questions.question: Why do the one-to-many relationships in the résumé imply a tree, and what does JSON do with that fact?

options.text: Each item belongs to exactly one résumé with no sideways links, so JSON makes the tree explicit
Because JSON supports only trees, the data has to be reshaped to fit the format
Because foreign key references between records always turn out to form cycles
Because a résumé is an ordered document that is read strictly from top to bottom

questions.explanation: The shape of the relationships, not the storage format, is what makes the tree.

questions.question: region_id and industry_id are IDs, not strings. Which advantages do standardized lists with a drop-down or autocompleter bring? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Consistent style and spelling, and no ambiguity when places share a name
Ease of updating — the name lives in one place, so a rename propagates
Localization support — standardized lists can be translated with the site
A smaller storage footprint, which is the main motivation for using IDs

questions.explanation: Stable IDs backed by standardized lists support consistent spelling, disambiguation, localization, centralized renaming, and broader search—for example, matching a region through a city inside it. Avoiding duplicated names and meanings is the main goal, not saving a few bytes.

optionExplanations.a: Selecting a canonical place or industry produces consistent spelling and distinguishes different places with the same display name. Free-text strings cannot reliably provide that identity.
optionExplanations.b: An ID references one canonical record, so changing its displayed name updates every profile that points to it. Duplicated strings would require finding and rewriting every copy.
optionExplanations.c: A stable identifier can map to different translated labels without changing the stored relationship. This separates identity from presentation language.
optionExplanations.d: IDs may save some bytes, but storage reduction is not the main reason for normalization. Consistency, unambiguous identity, centralized updates, localization, and better search are the important benefits.

questions.question: 'Should this field hold an ID or the text itself?' reduces to one underlying question. Which?

options.text: Performance: integer IDs are faster to compare and to index than strings
Duplication: an ID stores the meaning once; text duplicates it per record
Storage: IDs consume far fewer bytes than human-readable names
Security: IDs hide business meaning from anyone reading the data

questions.explanation: The choice is fundamentally about duplication. Storing an ID keeps the human-readable meaning in one canonical record and lets many records refer to it; embedding the text copies that meaning everywhere and makes later changes require coordinated updates.

questions.question: Why are meaningless IDs more stable than human-readable values?

options.text: Because an ID means nothing to humans, it never needs to change
Because IDs are assigned by the database, which never alters values
Because IDs are indexed, and index entries cannot be modified in place
Because IDs are globally unique across every system that shares them

questions.explanation: It can remain the same even if the information it identifies changes. Anything meaningful to humans may need to change, and if duplicated, all redundant copies must be updated, which incurs write overheads and risks inconsistencies. Meaninglessness is the source of stability.

questions.question: What does normalizing a schema mean, and how much practical interest do the normal form distinctions hold?

options.text: Removing duplication; the normal form distinctions are of little practical interest
Reaching at least third normal form, which is mandatory for correctness
Denormalizing selectively to improve read performance under load
Enforcing an explicit schema at write time on every table

questions.explanation: Normalization means storing each fact in one canonical place instead of duplicating it. Named normal forms refine that idea, but the practical question here is whether repeated values can drift apart and therefore should be referenced by ID.

questions.question: Why does normalizing repeated organization or region names into referenced records fit document databases poorly?

options.text: Because document databases cannot store identifiers as references
Because normalization requires the fixed schema documents lack
It creates many-to-one relationships, and document join support is weak
Because document databases provide no secondary indexes to join on

questions.explanation: Normalization replaces duplicated text with many-to-one references. That shape requires joins to recover the referenced information, while document databases are strongest when related data forms a self-contained tree and their join support is limited or product-specific.

questions.question: A profile references a region and an industry by ID, but the document database has no joins. What do you do, and why is this case forgiving?

options.text: Emulate the join in application code; the lists here are small enough to cache
Denormalize and accept the inconsistency, which is always an acceptable trade
Change database, since there is no workaround in application code at all
Use a materialized view, which every document database is said to support

questions.explanation: The lists of regions and industries are probably small and slow-changing enough to keep in memory. Nevertheless, the work of making the join is shifted from the database to the application code: it moved, it did not disappear.

questions.question: What commonly makes an initially suitable document model become awkward as an application grows?

options.text: New features add more relationships between separate documents
Every document inevitably becomes a smaller and simpler tree
Only data volume changes while relationships always stay fixed
The database automatically normalizes all nested documents

questions.explanation: New features tend to introduce links between previously separate entities. A document model can be an excellent initial fit for self-contained records, but increasing relationship density may make graph or relational querying more natural.

questions.question: One user writes a recommendation for another, displayed with the recommender's name and photo. Why must the recommendation hold a reference rather than a copy?

options.text: Because copies of images consume considerably more disk space
Because resolving a reference is faster than reading an inline copy
Because a photo update must show up in every past recommendation
Because the document model forbids duplicating another document's fields

questions.explanation: That requires a reference to the recommender's profile, not a copy of the name and photo. A copy freezes derived data that must stay live — the classic argument against denormalizing mutable, human-meaningful information.

questions.question: What is true of IBM's IMS? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It was the most popular database for business data processing in the 1970s
It was built for stock-keeping in the Apollo program, released commercially in 1968
It is still in use and maintained today, running on OS/390 on IBM mainframes
It was the first commercial database to implement the SQL language

questions.explanation: IMS stores records in a hierarchy: each record has one parent and may contain children. That tree-of-records structure resembles nested documents, making IMS a historical predecessor of modern document databases despite its very different era and interface.

optionExplanations.a: IMS dominated business data processing in the 1970s, showing that hierarchical databases were commercially important rather than a minor precursor. Its popularity is part of the historical comparison.
optionExplanations.b: IMS originated in inventory tracking for the Apollo program and became commercially available in 1968. The stock-keeping origin explains its early hierarchical record structure.
optionExplanations.c: IMS continued to be maintained and used on IBM mainframes such as OS/390 long after relational systems became dominant. “Old” does not mean the deployed system disappeared.
optionExplanations.d: IMS uses a hierarchical model and predates SQL's relational standardization; it was not the first commercial SQL implementation. Confusing its commercial importance with relational innovation mixes two database generations.

questions.question: Name the network model's other name, who standardized it, and the single structural change distinguishing it from the hierarchical model.

options.text: CODASYL, standardized by the Conference on Data Systems Languages; multiple parents
CODASYL, standardized by ANSI; records were permitted to have no parent at all
The relational model, standardized by IBM; records became formally unordered
The graph model, standardized by the W3C; records acquired type labels

questions.explanation: A record could have multiple parents instead of exactly one. That single relaxation is what let it model many-to-one and many-to-many relationships.

questions.question: How do CODASYL links differ from foreign keys, and what is an access path?

options.text: Links were pointer-like, stored on disk; the access path is the chain you must follow
Links were indexed foreign keys; the access path is a plan chosen by the optimizer
Links were symbolic record names; the access path is a sorted secondary index
Links were content hashes; the access path is the partition key used for routing

questions.explanation: The only way of accessing a record was to follow a path from a root record along these chains of links. Pointer-chasing as the only access method is what made the model rigid.

questions.question: How was a query performed in the CODASYL network model, and how did its own designers describe navigating it?

options.text: By moving a cursor through the database; members likened it to an n-dimensional space
By submitting a declarative query whose access path the optimizer selected
By writing SQL with recursive common table expressions over the links
By issuing map and reduce functions across the record chains

questions.explanation: Iterating over lists of records and following access paths. With many-to-many relationships the application code had to keep track of all the various relationships, holding access paths in the programmer's head.

questions.question: Give the honest defence of manual access path selection, and the argument that sank it.

options.text: For: best use of 1970s hardware, notably slow tape seeks. Against: inflexible code
For: it was strictly more expressive. Against: it ran slower than SQL did
For: it guaranteed consistency. Against: it could not scale to many machines
For: it was easier for COBOL programmers to learn. Against: poor tooling

questions.explanation: If you had no access path to the data you wanted, you had to rewrite the code, making it difficult to change an application's data model. Under 1970s constraints the hand-tuning was genuinely right — and the inflexibility still killed it.

questions.question: Compared with CODASYL's application-managed access paths, which freedoms did the relational model introduce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data is exposed as flat relations rather than nested records with application-visible traversal paths
Queries may select any rows matching a condition rather than following one predeclared access path
Applications can query by arbitrary columns, while the optimizer chooses indexes and access paths
Every insert must use a mandatory foreign-key path chosen by the application

questions.explanation: The relational model exposes tables and predicates while leaving physical access paths to the query optimizer. Foreign-key constraints may be used, but they are not the defining mechanism and applications do not manually navigate pointer chains.

optionExplanations.a: Relations expose rows and columns rather than application-visible pointer chains through nested records. That abstraction lets physical layout change without rewriting traversal code.
optionExplanations.b: A declarative predicate can select every row satisfying a condition without naming one predeclared route to each record. The engine is free to choose how to find the matches.
optionExplanations.c: Applications can filter or join on different columns, while indexes and join orders are selected by the optimizer. New access patterns therefore need not be hard-coded as cursor movements.
optionExplanations.d: Foreign keys are optional integrity constraints, not mandatory application-managed traversal paths for insertion. Requiring such navigation would recreate the CODASYL coupling the relational model removed.

questions.question: In what sense does a relational database still have access paths, and what is the big difference?

options.text: Index and join-order choice is the access path, but the optimizer makes it, not you
Relational engines dropped access paths entirely when SQL arrived
Access paths are declared in the schema and fixed when the table is created
Access paths are selected by the client driver before the query is sent

questions.explanation: So if you want to query your data in new ways you can just declare a new index, and queries will automatically use whichever indexes are most appropriate, without changing the queries. The consequence: it became much easier to add new features.

questions.question: Query optimizers are complicated beasts that consumed many years of research and development effort. Reconstruct the argument that this was still the right trade.

options.text: You build the optimizer once and every application using the database benefits
Optimizers were cheap to build compared with the application code they replaced
Optimizers let the same workload run on considerably cheaper hardware
Optimizers removed the need to maintain secondary indexes by hand

questions.explanation: Hand-coding one access path may be easier than building a general optimizer, but an optimizer's cost is paid once by the database vendor and its benefits are reused by every application and query. The abstraction amortizes sophisticated planning across many users.

questions.question: In what one aspect did document databases revert to the hierarchical model, and in what respect are they not different from relational databases?

options.text: They reverted fully, access paths included, and so differ from relational entirely
They reverted in query style, becoming imperative rather than declarative
Only in nesting records within a parent; cross-references work the same in both
They reverted in ordering, making stored records position-dependent again

questions.explanation: For many-to-one and many-to-many relationships both families reference the related item by a unique identifier — a foreign key in relational, a document reference in document databases — resolved at read time. To date, document databases have not followed the path of CODASYL.

questions.question: When comparing relational and document data models, which topics are intentionally outside this comparison?

options.text: Fault-tolerance properties and handling of concurrency
Query language expressiveness and indexing strategy
Licensing terms and total cost of ownership
Schema enforcement and physical storage locality

questions.explanation: The comparison concerns data-model shape and query ergonomics. Fault tolerance and concurrency are separate design dimensions: systems using either model can make different choices for replication, transactions, and failure handling.

questions.question: Which arguments favour the document model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Schema flexibility
Better performance due to locality
For some applications, closeness to the application's own data structures
Better support for joins and many-to-many relationships

questions.explanation: The last one favours the relational model — those are precisely the shapes document models handle worst.

optionExplanations.a: Documents can accommodate records with varying fields and nested shapes without first migrating every row to one rigid structure. That flexibility helps when data is heterogeneous or externally controlled.
optionExplanations.b: Keeping a self-contained aggregate in one document can fetch it with one read instead of several joins. The benefit is conditional: it weakens when only a small portion of a large document is needed.
optionExplanations.c: For applications already manipulating nested objects, a document can closely match the in-memory shape and reduce object-relational translation. This is strongest for tree-like, self-contained records.
optionExplanations.d: Joins and many-to-many relationships are strengths of the relational model, not the document model. Documents often require denormalization or application-side joins for those relationship shapes.

questions.question: Define shredding, and when is it the wrong move?

options.text: Splitting a document into many tables, giving cumbersome schemas and complex code
Compressing documents before storage, which is the recommended practice
Partitioning documents across machines, which is essential at any scale
Stripping unused fields from documents, which is neither good nor bad

questions.explanation: The cost lands when the data really is a tree of one-to-many relationships where typically the entire tree is loaded at once. Shredding is the relational technique that the document model exists to avoid.

questions.question: State the document model's limitation on referring to nested items, and the condition under which it stops mattering.

options.text: You cannot address a nested item directly, only positionally; fine if nesting is shallow
Nested items cannot be indexed at all, which is a problem in every application
Nested items can only be replaced wholesale, never updated field by field
Nested items are limited to three levels of depth by the storage format

questions.explanation: You need to say something like 'the second item in the list of positions for user 251' — much like an access path in the hierarchical model. The positional reference is the hierarchical model's access path resurfacing in miniature.

questions.question: Give an example of an application where poor join support genuinely doesn't matter.

options.text: An analytics application recording which events occurred at which time
A social network, because friendship edges are always symmetric
An e-commerce catalogue, because products are independent of one another
A banking ledger, because its transactions are strictly append-only

questions.explanation: Many-to-many relationships may never be needed there. Whether weak joins matter depends entirely on the application's relationship shapes.

questions.question: If your application does use many-to-many relationships, which two workarounds exist in a document model, and at what cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Denormalize to avoid joins — but the application must keep copies consistent
Emulate joins in application code — usually slower than the database's own
Adopt a graph query language inside the document database itself
Store every relationship as a positional reference into the parent document

questions.explanation: In such cases, using a document model can lead to significantly more complex application code and worse performance, since joins inside the database run in specialized code.

optionExplanations.a: Duplicating related data inside documents can make reads local, but every copy must be updated consistently when the source changes. The avoided join is exchanged for write coordination and inconsistency risk.
optionExplanations.b: Application code can fetch referenced documents and combine them, but this adds round trips and executes less specialized join logic. Database-native joins usually have more optimization opportunities.
optionExplanations.c: A particular product might add graph-like operators, but that is not a general document-model workaround and effectively introduces another query model. The two stated choices are denormalization or application-side joining.
optionExplanations.d: Positional references are fragile because inserting or reordering elements changes positions, and they recreate application-managed access paths. Stable IDs are needed for durable cross-document relationships.

questions.question: For highly interconnected data, how do the document, relational and graph models rank?

options.text: Document awkward, relational acceptable, graph most natural
Graph awkward, document acceptable, relational most natural
All three are equally suitable for interconnected data
Relational awkward, graph acceptable, document most natural

questions.explanation: But it is not possible to say in general which data model leads to simpler application code — it depends on the kinds of relationships that exist between data items.

questions.question: Which statement accurately compares schema enforcement for document stores and relational JSON or XML columns?

options.text: Both are often flexible, while relational JSON or XML can also be validated when configured
Both always reject fields that were not declared before any record was written
Only document databases enforce schemas; relational JSON and XML never can
Relational XML validation is mandatory in every database and configuration

questions.explanation: These categories do not share one universal enforcement rule. Document stores and JSON columns are often schema-on-read, while some relational systems can validate XML—or JSON—against a declared schema when configured. Distinguish available validation from mandatory enforcement.

questions.question: Why is 'schemaless' the wrong word, and what are the two accurate terms?

options.text: Reading code assumes structure, so the schema is implicit: schema-on-read vs schema-on-write
All databases have schemas, so the terms are strict-schema and loose-schema
Schemas live in the driver, so the terms are client-schema and server-schema
The word is trademarked, so the accepted terms are flexible and rigid

questions.explanation: Schema-on-read means structure is implicit and only interpreted when data is read; schema-on-write is the traditional relational approach, where the schema is explicit and the database ensures all written data conforms. The schema does not disappear, it relocates.

questions.question: Map schema-on-read and schema-on-write onto programming language type checking. Which is better?

options.text: Read is dynamic runtime checking, write is static compile-time; no right answer
Read is static typing, write is dynamic typing; static always wins out
The closer analogy is manual versus automatic memory management
Both map to dynamic typing, differing only in the available tooling

questions.explanation: Schema-on-read resembles dynamic runtime checking because interpretation happens when data is consumed; schema-on-write resembles static checking because structure is enforced before storage. Neither is universally better: the choice depends on data uniformity, ownership, and how safely change can be coordinated.

questions.question: You store each user's full name in one field and now want first and last name separately. What do you do in a document database?

options.text: Write new documents with the new fields and handle old ones in read code
Run a bulk migration that rewrites every existing document in place
Declare a new schema version and reindex the whole collection
Drop the collection and recreate it with the new field layout

questions.explanation: No migration and no cutover date needed. The read path absorbs the heterogeneity, which is the practical meaning of schema-on-read.

questions.question: Schema changes have a reputation for being slow and requiring downtime. How deserved is it, and what is the exception?

options.text: Not entirely deserved: most databases ALTER TABLE in milliseconds; MySQL copies the table
Fully deserved: every relational database rewrites the table on a schema change
The reputation applies only to PostgreSQL, whose DDL takes table locks
Schema changes are effectively instantaneous on all modern databases

questions.explanation: MySQL copying the entire table can mean minutes or even hours of downtime. Tools exist to work around the limitation, but the caveat is real.

questions.question: Between ALTER TABLE and UPDATE, which is the real performance problem, and what is the escape hatch?

options.text: ALTER TABLE; the escape hatch is to put the new column in a separate table
UPDATE, since every row is rewritten; leave the default NULL and fill on read
ALTER TABLE and UPDATE cost the same, and the rewrite is unavoidable
On contemporary server hardware the cost of either is negligible

questions.explanation: Note where this lands: the relational escape hatch is to behave exactly like schema-on-read, filling the value in at read time as a document database would.

questions.question: When is data heterogeneous enough that schema-on-read genuinely wins? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Many different types of object, impractical to give each its own table
Structure determined by external systems you do not control, which may change
The dataset has grown too large for the database to index efficiently
The team lacks the SQL expertise to maintain an explicit schema

questions.explanation: The balanced conclusion: where all records are expected to have the same structure, schemas are a useful mechanism for documenting and enforcing that structure. Otherwise a schema may hurt more than it helps.

optionExplanations.a: When a collection contains many genuinely different object types, a table per type may become unwieldy and sparse common tables may misrepresent them. Interpreting each record according to its own shape can then be simpler.
optionExplanations.b: Externally controlled producers can change fields without coordinating a database migration. Schema-on-read lets consumers interpret multiple versions, though they must still validate what they receive.
optionExplanations.c: Dataset size affects indexing strategy and partitioning, not whether records share a stable structure. A large uniform dataset can still benefit from an explicit schema.
optionExplanations.d: Team familiarity with SQL is a staffing issue rather than evidence that the data is heterogeneous. Avoiding schema because of missing expertise sacrifices documentation and validation without fixing the underlying skills gap.

questions.question: Physically, why does a document have good locality, and what is the relational contrast?

options.text: Documents are always held in memory, whereas rows must be read from disk
Documents are compressed on disk, so fewer bytes cross the storage bus
A document is one continuous string; split tables need several index lookups
Documents avoid indexes entirely, so no lookup cost is paid at all

questions.explanation: Encoded as JSON, XML, or a binary variant such as MongoDB's BSON. Multiple index lookups may require more disk seeks. Locality is a physical property of contiguous storage, not a property of the document model as such.

questions.question: Which conditions and costs bound the locality argument, and which design rules follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The advantage applies only if you need large parts of the document at once
The whole document is loaded even for a small portion, wasteful when large
Updates usually rewrite the whole document, so keep documents small
Locality only pays off on SSDs, not on spinning disks with slow seeks

questions.explanation: Locality helps only when a read needs a large portion of the document. Reading one field may still load the whole object, and size-changing updates often rewrite it, so documents should remain small and avoid unbounded growth. These costs substantially narrow the workloads that benefit.

optionExplanations.a: Locality helps when a request needs much of the aggregate because one contiguous document read replaces several lookups or joins. If only one field is needed, reading the rest becomes waste.
optionExplanations.b: Many document stores load the complete encoded document even for a small requested portion. Large documents therefore amplify I/O, parsing, and memory costs for narrow reads.
optionExplanations.c: Changing a document's encoded size often requires rewriting it, so frequently growing or very large documents make updates expensive. Keeping aggregates bounded preserves the intended locality benefit.
optionExplanations.d: Locality also matters on spinning disks, where avoiding seeks can be especially valuable; it is not an SSD-only effect. Hardware changes the magnitude, not the existence, of the trade-off.

questions.question: Match each system to its locality mechanism: Spanner, Oracle, Bigtable.

options.text: Spanner row interleaving; Oracle index clusters; Bigtable column families
All three of them achieve locality by nesting documents inside a parent document
Spanner uses column families, Bigtable interleaves rows, and Oracle stores documents
Locality is exclusive to the document model, so none of the three achieves it

questions.explanation: Spanner's schema declares the interleaving; the Bigtable model is used in Cassandra and HBase. The idea of grouping related data together for locality is not limited to the document model.

questions.question: Which relational databases support XML and JSON, and since when?

options.text: XML since the mid-2000s except MySQL; JSON in PostgreSQL 9.3, MySQL 5.7, DB2 10.5
XML since the mid-1990s in all systems; JSON only ever in PostgreSQL
Relational databases dropped XML support once JSON became popular
MySQL led on XML support, while PostgreSQL still has no JSON type

questions.explanation: Relational systems added XML functions, indexes, and partial-update support, and later adopted native JSON types as JSON became common in APIs. This shows that data models borrow useful features from one another rather than remaining fixed, isolated categories.

questions.question: What are document databases adding, and what caveat applies?

options.text: RethinkDB has joins and MongoDB drivers resolve references — but client-side, so slower
They are adding complete SQL support at no measurable performance cost
They are adding enforced schemas, which removes the need for joins
They are adding nothing; convergence between the families runs one way only

questions.explanation: A client-side join requires additional network round-trips and is less optimized than one performed in the database. Convergence is real but asymmetric in cost.

questions.question: Are relational and document databases converging, and why is nesting a return rather than an invention?

options.text: The two families are diverging, exactly as Codd's paper predicted they would
Convergence is a mistake that dilutes the strengths of both models
Convergence is good, and Codd's nonsimple domains already allowed nested relations
Codd forbade nested values, which makes convergence a genuine modern invention

questions.explanation: The models complement each other, so applications can use whichever combination of features fits. Codd's nonsimple domains let a value in a row be a nested relation rather than atomic — over 30 years before document databases arrived. A hybrid is a good route for the future.

questions.question: Besides a data model, what did the relational model bring, and what is the contrast with IMS and CODASYL?

options.text: Declarative querying via SQL, where IMS and CODASYL used imperative APIs
Transactions, which neither IMS nor CODASYL provided in any form
Indexes, where IMS and CODASYL relied on scanning every record
Replication, where IMS and CODASYL were strictly single-node systems

questions.explanation: Applications on IMS and CODASYL typically used COBOL code to iterate over records one at a time. The declarative turn is arguably the more consequential half of the relational model's contribution.

questions.question: What distinguishes an imperative query language from a declarative one?

options.text: Imperative orders operations; declarative states the pattern wanted, not the how
Imperative languages are compiled; declarative languages are interpreted
Imperative languages use loops; declarative languages use recursion instead
Imperative languages are statically typed; declarative languages are untyped

questions.explanation: A declarative language specifies what conditions the results must meet and how it should be transformed, leaving the query optimizer to decide how. 'What, not how' is the dividing line, and the optimizer is what the gap makes room for.

questions.question: A declarative query language has one obvious advantage and one more important, structural one. What is the structural one?

options.text: That it is more concise and easier to work with than an imperative API
That it hides engine internals, so performance can improve without query changes
That it is considerably easier to teach to new engineers
That queries can be checked for errors statically before they run

questions.explanation: Conciseness is the obvious win; engine evolvability without query changes is the structural one.

questions.question: The database wants to reclaim disk space by moving records around, changing the order in which animals appear. Why can it do this safely under SQL but not under imperative code?

options.text: SQL guarantees no ordering, so reordering is safe; imperative code might depend on it
Because SQL takes a table lock for the whole duration of the compaction
Because imperative query code has no direct access to the on-disk layout
Because SQL always keeps its records in their original insertion order

questions.explanation: With imperative code the database can never be sure whether the code relies on ordering. The fact that SQL is more limited in functionality gives the database much more room for automatic optimizations — less expressive power buys more freedom to optimize.

questions.question: Which hardware trend favours declarative languages, and what argument follows?

options.text: CPUs gain cores rather than clock speed; imperative order resists parallelization
Disks are getting faster, so the choice of query plan matters much less
Memory is getting cheaper, so entire datasets now fit in RAM
Networks are getting faster, which favours joins on the client side

questions.explanation: Processor performance increasingly grows through additional cores rather than much faster single cores. A declarative query specifies the desired result without fixing execution order, giving the engine freedom to partition and parallelize work across those cores.

questions.question: In CSS, what does the selector `li.selected > p` match?

options.text: A `p` directly inside an `li.selected` element
Every `p` anywhere below any `li`, regardless of its class
Every `li` that contains a `p` somewhere among its descendants
Only the first `p` element that appears anywhere in the document

questions.explanation: The `>` combinator requires a direct parent-child relationship, and `.selected` requires the parent `li` to have that class. Without that combinator, `li.selected p` would match a `p` at any depth below the selected list item.

questions.question: The JavaScript DOM version of that styling 'is awful'. Beyond being longer, which two serious problems does it have? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It doesn't undo itself — removing the class leaves the element blue until reload
It blocks engine improvements — a new DOM API means rewriting the code
It is unable to select elements by their class name at all
It runs correctly in only one particular browser rendering engine

questions.explanation: With CSS the browser automatically detects when the rule no longer applies; browsers can also improve CSS performance without breaking compatibility, whereas taking advantage of document.getElementsByClassName means editing the code. The second problem is the database argument transplanted to the browser.

optionExplanations.a: Imperative JavaScript sets a style once but does not automatically reverse it when the element stops matching. Declarative CSS continuously relates appearance to the current DOM state, so removal of the class removes the rule's effect.
optionExplanations.b: Imperative code commits to a particular traversal API and algorithm, so adopting a faster new API requires code changes. A CSS engine can optimize rule evaluation internally while preserving the same declaration.
optionExplanations.c: DOM APIs can select elements by class, including `getElementsByClassName`; inability to select them is not the problem. The issue is maintaining the result and coupling code to the traversal mechanism.
optionExplanations.d: Standard DOM manipulation is not inherently limited to one rendering engine. Browser differences can exist, but the stated architectural problems are stale effects and blocked implementation optimization.

questions.question: Why is MapReduce neither fully declarative nor a conventional imperative query API?

options.text: The framework controls iteration, but users supply imperative map and reduce functions
It is declarative in exactly the same way as SQL and contains no user code
Users manually navigate every stored record and choose every access path
Its map phase is declarative while its reduce phase is always relational

questions.explanation: The framework decides how to distribute, schedule, and repeatedly invoke user functions, but the functions themselves contain executable logic. Their names come from functional programming: map is also called collect, while reduce is also called fold or inject.

questions.question: In MongoDB's shark-counting `mapReduce` example, what does the declarative species filter do before the JavaScript map function runs?

options.text: That the filter is declarative — a MongoDB extension, not part of MapReduce
That filters must always be written inside the body of the map function
That MapReduce has no way of filtering input records at all
That filtering necessarily happens during the reduce step

questions.explanation: The query filter selects only shark documents, and MongoDB calls the map function once for each match. Filtering is a MongoDB extension around MapReduce rather than logic that must be embedded in the map or reduce callback.

questions.question: A collection holds two records for the same month, with counts of 3 and 4. In a MapReduce job that sums per month, how many times is map called, how many times is reduce called, and what does reduce receive?

options.text: map per document emits ('1995-12', 3) and ('1995-12', 4); reduce('1995-12', [3,4]) returns 7
map runs once for the pair, emitting ('1995-12', 7), and reduce is never called
reduce runs once per document, accumulating a running total that reaches 7
map emits 3 and 4 under separate keys, and reduce returns them unchanged

questions.explanation: Values emitted under the same key are grouped and handed to reduce once.

questions.question: Which restriction lets a framework relocate, reorder, and retry MapReduce functions safely?

options.text: They use only their input data and produce no external side effects
They must be JavaScript functions that can freely query the database
They may perform side effects as long as each worker has a unique ID
They must be declarative expressions and cannot call library functions

questions.explanation: Pure functions depend only on their input and do not mutate external state, so rerunning one does not duplicate a side effect and moving it to another worker does not change its meaning. They may still parse strings, call libraries, and perform arbitrary calculations.

questions.question: Why did MongoDB add a declarative aggregation pipeline alongside MapReduce?

options.text: MapReduce could not distribute work, so the pipeline added worker scheduling
Coordinating two JavaScript functions was awkward, and declarative stages are easier to optimize
JavaScript support was removed, so the pipeline became the only way to read documents
MapReduce could not represent any filtering, grouping, or aggregation operation

questions.explanation: MongoDB 2.2 added the pipeline because a sequence of declarative stages is usually easier to write and optimize than two coordinated JavaScript functions. Its expressiveness resembles a subset of SQL, illustrating how useful declarative ideas reappeared in NoSQL systems.

questions.question: Using relationship shape alone, when is the document model appropriate and when does a graph become natural?

options.text: Documents fit trees or no relationships; graphs fit as connections grow complex
Graphs fit tree-structured data; documents fit heavily interconnected data
The choice between them depends only on the total volume of data
Graphs are preferable as soon as any many-to-many relationship appears

questions.explanation: Relational databases can handle simple cases of many-to-many, but as connections within your data become more complex it becomes more natural to model the data as a graph. A clean decision rule based purely on relationship shape, not on scale.

questions.question: Give the two kinds of objects in a graph with their synonyms.

options.text: Vertices (nodes, entities) and edges (relationships, arcs)
Rows (also called tuples) and links (stored on-disk pointers)
Documents (also called records) and references (foreign keys)
Subjects (also called heads) and predicates (also called tails)

questions.explanation: The three canonical examples: social graphs (vertices are people, edges indicate who knows whom), the web graph (vertices are pages, edges are HTML links), and road or rail networks (vertices are junctions, edges are roads). Well-known algorithms include shortest path and PageRank.

questions.question: Social graphs, the web graph and road networks share a property. Name it, and give the equally powerful alternative use.

options.text: They are homogeneous; but graphs also store wholly different object types together
They are all directed, and a graph model cannot represent undirected edges
They are all acyclic, and the graph model requires acyclicity to work
They are all small enough to be held entirely in main memory

questions.explanation: Social, web, and road graphs are homogeneous examples because their vertices usually represent one broad kind of entity. Property graphs can also mix people, places, events, and comments in one graph, using labels and properties to distinguish them.

questions.question: Which two graph data models are commonly contrasted?

options.text: Property graphs and triple stores
Relational graphs and document graphs
Hierarchical trees and CODASYL networks
Property graphs and adjacency matrices

questions.explanation: Property-graph implementations include Neo4j, Titan, and InfiniteGraph; triple stores include Datomic and AllegroGraph. Declarative languages span Cypher for property graphs, SPARQL for RDF triples, and Datalog as a more general rule-based approach.

questions.question: What core information does an edge store in a property graph?

options.text: An ID, tail and head vertex IDs, a label, and properties
Only the two endpoint IDs, with no label or edge properties
A collection of properties with no endpoints or direction
Only a traversal weight and the label of its source vertex

questions.explanation: The tail identifies where a directed edge starts and the head where it ends; the label names the relationship and properties describe it. Vertices separately have IDs, incoming and outgoing edge references, and their own properties, with indexes enabling traversal in either direction.

questions.question: Which are the three important aspects of the property graph model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Any vertex can have an edge to any other vertex; no schema restricts associations
From any vertex you can efficiently find incoming and outgoing edges alike
Different edge labels let one graph hold several kinds of information cleanly
Edges may only be traversed in the direction in which they were created

questions.explanation: Property graphs allow unrestricted vertex-to-vertex edges, efficient traversal in either direction, and labels that distinguish relationship types. Those properties let one graph represent heterogeneous, highly connected information without fixing one hierarchy in advance.

optionExplanations.a: Property graphs allow an edge between arbitrary vertices without a schema fixing one hierarchy. That freedom supports evolving, heterogeneous relationships such as people, places, organizations, and events.
optionExplanations.b: Indexes on both tail and head endpoints let a traversal efficiently follow outgoing or incoming edges. Direction labels the relationship but does not restrict which way a query may navigate.
optionExplanations.c: Labels distinguish relationship meanings such as `BORN_IN`, `LIVES_IN`, or `MARRIED_TO` within one graph. Queries can select the relevant type without separating every relationship into another database.
optionExplanations.d: Directed edges record a tail and head, but graph stores normally support lookup from either endpoint. Creation direction expresses semantics; it does not force all traversals to move only forward.

questions.question: Which of these would be difficult to express in a traditional relational schema? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Different regional structures per country — départements and régions versus counties and states
Quirks of history, such as a country existing within another country
Varying granularity — a residence given as a city, a birthplace only as a state
The total count of people currently represented anywhere in the graph

questions.explanation: Irregular, heterogeneous, variably-grained structure is the graph model's home territory.

optionExplanations.a: Administrative hierarchies differ by country, so one fixed set of nullable relational columns fits poorly and requires many exceptions. A graph can add the appropriate place types and `WITHIN` edges per region.
optionExplanations.b: Historical arrangements can violate a simple tree, such as one country being contained within another in a special sense. Flexible edges represent the exception without redesigning a universal hierarchy.
optionExplanations.c: A graph can link a person to a city in one case and only a state in another while preserving both as locations. Fixed relational levels make this variable granularity awkward.
optionExplanations.d: Counting all represented people is a straightforward aggregate over person rows or vertices. Irregular relationship structure is irrelevant to that simple global count.

questions.question: How would you extend the graph to answer 'what is safe for each person to eat', and what general property does that show?

options.text: Add allergen vertices and allergy edges, linked to foods; graphs are good for evolvability
Add an allergy column to each person vertex; graphs need no schema changes
Keep allergies in a relational table alongside; hybrids are always necessary
Encode allergies as edge properties only; edges are cheaper than vertices

questions.explanation: Link the allergens with a set of vertices showing which foods contain which substances. As you add features, a graph can easily be extended to accommodate changes in your application's data structures — evolvability by extension rather than migration.

questions.question: What is Cypher, who made it, and where does the name come from?

options.text: A declarative property-graph language from Neo4j, named after a Matrix character
An imperative traversal API from Titan, named after cryptographic ciphers
A triple-store query language standardized by the W3C for RDF data
A MapReduce dialect created at Google for graph-shaped datasets

questions.explanation: Cypher is Neo4j's declarative query language for property graphs. Its name references the character Cypher from The Matrix, not cryptography; pattern syntax states the graph shape to match while the engine chooses the traversal plan.

questions.question: In Cypher, what does the directed pattern `(Idaho)-[:WITHIN]->(USA)` create?

options.text: An edge labeled WITHIN, with Idaho as tail and USA as head
An edge labeled WITHIN, with USA as tail and Idaho as head
Two undirected edges labeled WITHIN between Idaho and USA
A property named WITHIN set on the Idaho vertex

questions.explanation: The arrow runs from Idaho to USA, so Idaho is the tail and USA the head of a `WITHIN` edge. Symbolic vertex names let later clauses refer to the same vertices without repeating their properties.

questions.question: A Cypher MATCH finds persons with a BORN_IN edge leading to a place connected by a chain of zero or more outgoing WITHIN edges to a Location named 'United States', and a LIVES_IN edge leading similarly to 'Europe'. What does it return?

options.text: Names of people who emigrated from the United States to Europe
Names of people born in Europe who now live in the United States
Names of everyone in the graph having any BORN_IN edge at all
Names of all Location vertices inside the United States and Europe

questions.explanation: Both conditions must hold for the same person. The variable-length WITHIN*0.. is what lets a birthplace at any granularity — city, state, region — roll up to the country. MATCH finds patterns, with the tail at the arrow's start and the head at its point.

questions.question: For people and places linked by `BORN_IN`, `LIVES_IN`, and `WITHIN`, who chooses how a declarative emigration query traverses the graph?

options.text: Application code must choose depth-first or breadth-first traversal
Only a full scan of all people is possible
The optimizer chooses the starting point and traversal plan
The query must state one fixed traversal order

questions.explanation: A declarative graph query describes the required relationship pattern, not the traversal order. The optimizer can scan people or begin from indexed location vertices and walk incoming `WITHIN`, `BORN_IN`, and `LIVES_IN` edges, depending on estimated cost.

questions.question: Can you query graph data with SQL, and what is the precise reason for the difficulty?

options.text: Yes but awkwardly: graph traversal needs a variable number of joins, unknown in advance
SQL cannot express traversal at all, so a graph database is always required
Yes trivially, because a join and an edge traversal are exactly equivalent
Yes, but only for undirected graphs whose edge labels are all uniform

questions.explanation: In a relational database you usually know in advance which joins you need; a WITHIN edge may point to a street, a city, a district, a region, a state, and so on. Variable-length paths are the shape SQL handles worst, which is why recursive common table expressions exist.

questions.question: Give the form of a triple and name its three parts with an example.

options.text: (subject, predicate, object) — as in (Jim, likes, bananas)
(vertex, edge, vertex) — with the predicate left implicit
(key, value, timestamp) — as in a versioned key-value store
(table, row, column) — addressing one cell of a relation

questions.explanation: Jim is the subject, “likes” is the predicate, and bananas is the object. Triple stores express many of the same ideas as property graphs with different terminology, but their RDF ecosystem and SPARQL query language make the representation independently useful.

questions.question: The subject of a triple is a vertex. The object is one of two things. Which, and what does the predicate mean in each case? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A primitive value — then predicate and object are a property key and value, as in (lucy, age, 33)
Another vertex — then the predicate is an edge label, subject the tail, object the head
A nested triple, which is what makes the whole model recursive
A reference to an RDF document that is stored on another server

questions.explanation: As in (lucy, marriedTo, alain), where marriedTo is the label of the edge. The object's type is what distinguishes a property from an edge in the triple-store model.

optionExplanations.a: When the object is a primitive, the predicate names an attribute and the object supplies its value. Thus `(lucy, age, 33)` corresponds to a property key-value pair on Lucy's vertex.
optionExplanations.b: When the object identifies another vertex, the predicate names the relationship; the subject is the edge tail and the object is its head. This is how triples represent graph edges.
optionExplanations.c: Basic RDF triples contain a subject, predicate, and object; an ordinary object is not recursively another complete triple. More advanced RDF-star representations exist, but they are not the model described here.
optionExplanations.d: An object may be a URI identifying a vertex, but it need not point to a remotely stored RDF document or resolve over the network. URIs can function simply as globally unique names.

questions.question: In Turtle notation, what does '_:someName' mean, and what does the semicolon do?

options.text: A local name, meaningless outside the file; the semicolon adds facts about one subject
A globally unique URI declaration; the semicolon terminates the statement
A predicate marker; the semicolon separates one subject from the next
A literal string value; the semicolon begins a trailing comment

questions.explanation: It is used only because we otherwise have nothing to refer to the vertex by. Turtle is a subset of Notation3 (N3). Whether a predicate represents an edge or a property is determined by the object: a string literal gives a property, another vertex gives an edge.

questions.question: State the semantic web's core idea, what RDF was for, and whether it worked.

options.text: Replace HTML with XML; RDF was a styling language; it largely succeeded
Also publish machine-readable data; RDF was the shared format; overhyped and unrealized
Build one global graph database; RDF was its storage engine; judged premature
Standardize SQL across the web; RDF was the wire protocol; still ongoing

questions.explanation: The idea is simple and reasonable, and RDF was meant to let data from different sites combine into a web of data — but it came with a dizzying plethora of acronyms, overly complex standards proposals, and hubris, though good work came out of it. The triple-store model is completely independent of the semantic web: Datomic makes no such claim, technically using 5-tuples whose two extra fields are versioning metadata.

questions.question: Why are RDF subjects, predicates and objects often URIs, and must they resolve?

options.text: For internet-wide exchange: a URI predicate avoids collisions, and need not resolve
Because RDF requires every identifier to be fetchable over HTTP to be valid
Because URIs compress better than plain strings in the stored representation
Because the SPARQL grammar only accepts URIs in predicate position

questions.explanation: If you combine your data with someone else's and they used the same word with a different meaning, you won't get a conflict, since their predicate is really a different URI. It is simply a namespace, declared once as a prefix at the top of the file. RDF also has an XML form, but Turtle/N3 is easier on the eyes, and Apache Jena converts between formats.

questions.question: What does SPARQL stand for?

options.text: SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language
Structured Parallel Query Language, said 'spar-cue-el'; it postdates Cypher
Semantic Property And Relationship Query Language; unrelated to Cypher entirely
SPARQL Pattern And RDF Query Layer; Cypher is the older of the two languages

questions.explanation: SPARQL stands for SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language and is usually pronounced “sparkle.” It predates Cypher and influenced Cypher's declarative graph-pattern style, although SPARQL targets RDF triples while Cypher targets property graphs.

questions.question: When expressing the same graph-pattern query in SPARQL and Cypher, which equivalences hold? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The query is even more concise in SPARQL; its variables start with a question mark
RDF uses predicates for both properties and edges, so one syntax matches both
SPARQL has no way at all to express variable-length path traversal
SPARQL requires an explicit join clause where Cypher manages without one

questions.explanation: SPARQL variables begin with `?`, and RDF represents both attributes and relationships as predicate triples, allowing one pattern syntax for both. This can make the equivalent query concise even though the underlying RDF and property-graph models differ.

optionExplanations.a: SPARQL variables use a `?` prefix, and its triple-pattern syntax can express the same relationship pattern compactly. Concision comes from matching the RDF representation directly, not from omitting semantics.
optionExplanations.b: RDF represents both an attribute and a relationship with a predicate, so the same subject-predicate-object pattern matches either. Property graphs usually distinguish vertex properties from edges more explicitly.
optionExplanations.c: SPARQL can express variable-length paths using property-path operators such as repetition. Claiming it has no path mechanism confuses basic triple patterns with the full query language.
optionExplanations.d: Adjacent SPARQL graph patterns share variables and thereby express joins without a separate `JOIN` clause. The optimizer chooses how to execute those matches just as in other declarative languages.

questions.question: Are graph databases the second coming of CODASYL in disguise? Which differences rule that out? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Schema — CODASYL fixed which record type nests in which; graphs impose no such rule
Reaching a record — CODASYL forced path traversal; graphs allow direct ID or index lookup
Ordering — CODASYL children were an ordered set; graph vertices and edges are unordered
Storage — CODASYL wrote links to disk whereas graph databases are memory-only

questions.explanation: The answer to the question is No. The fourth genuine difference is query style: CODASYL queries were all imperative, whereas graph databases also support declarative languages. In-memory storage is not a difference — both store on disk.

optionExplanations.a: CODASYL schemas fixed which record types could nest under others, while property graphs allow arbitrary vertex-to-vertex edges. That makes graph structure far easier to extend.
optionExplanations.b: CODASYL applications had to start at an access point and follow paths; graph databases can also locate a vertex directly by ID or indexed property. Traversal is an option rather than the only access mechanism.
optionExplanations.c: CODASYL child records formed an ordered set, making position part of its navigation model. Graph edges and vertices have no inherent order unless an application stores one explicitly.
optionExplanations.d: Graph databases are not memory-only; they commonly persist vertices and edges to disk just as CODASYL systems persisted records and links. Storage medium is not the differentiating feature.

questions.question: Which systems are concrete examples of Datalog use?

options.text: Datomic and Cascalog
Neo4j and Gremlin
PostgreSQL and MySQL
MongoDB and CouchDB

questions.explanation: Datalog was studied academically in the 1980s and helped establish ideas used by later query languages. Datomic uses a Clojure-style syntax, while Cascalog brings Datalog-like queries to large Hadoop datasets; Datalog itself is a restricted subset of Prolog.

questions.question: How does Datalog's notation relate to the triple-store model?

options.text: Similar but generalized: a triple is written predicate(subject, object)
It writes each triple as subject(predicate, object) instead
It abandons triples for an unrelated relational notation
It writes each triple as object(subject, predicate)

questions.explanation: Datalog generalizes the triple notation as `predicate(subject, object)`. Facts and derived rules use the same form, which makes recursive relationship queries composable rather than requiring explicit traversal code.

questions.question: Cypher and SPARQL jump in right away with SELECT. What does Datalog do instead, and what is the payoff?

options.text: It compiles down to SQL, so the payoff is portability across engines
